claim: OUR CALCULATION: about a spoonful (about seven grams) of sodium borohydride makes enough electricity to charge a phone
source_quote: they are less efficient at generating electricity alone (37%–42%)
note: OUR CALCULATION (gate has no such status; label it OUR CALCULATION on screen). Inputs: (1) NaBH4 + 2 H2O -> NaBO2 + 4 H2 (DRDO patent WO2017145068A1). (2) NaBH4 molar mass 37.84 g/mol (PubChem CID 4311764); H2 2.016 g/mol. (3) H2 LHV about 120 MJ/kg (National Academies, nap.nationalacademies.org/read/10922/chapter/240: 'Hydrogen’s Lower Heating Value (LHV) is approximately 120 MJ/kg'). (4) PAFC electrical efficiency 37-42% (US DOE, this URL). (5) Phone: 5,000 mAh typical (Samsung India Galaxy M05 spec) x 3.7 V nominal Li-ion (Battery University BU-205: NMC '3.60V, 3.70V nominal') = 18.5 Wh. Arithmetic: 1 g NaBH4 -> 4 x 2.016 / 37.84 = 0.213 g H2 (half of it from the water) -> 0.213 x 120 kJ = 25.6 kJ = 7.1 Wh chemical -> x 0.37-0.42 = 2.6-3.0 Wh electricity. 18.5 Wh / 2.6-3.0 = 6.2-7.0 g; allowing about 15% charging loss (our assumption) 7.3-8.3 g. VERDICT: 'about a spoonful, seven or eight grams' is honest for a 5-10 g spoonful; 'a teaspoon' alone would be on the small side. Ideal-case figure: ignores the plant's own power use and assumes the water's hydrogen is captured; say 'on paper' or 'in theory'. Oxygen comes from the LOX tank.
